query: Which method can be used for concurrent strength–ductility improvement, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying a tailored thermomechanical treatment (multistep rolling followed by controlled annealing) will concurrently increase strength and ductility in metallic alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or conventionally processed metallic alloy with relatively coarse grains and limited dislocation substructure
generation.intervention: Multistep rolling at predetermined strain rates and reductions per pass followed by controlled annealing at optimized temperatures
generation.conditions: Vary rolling reductions (e.g., 20–40% per pass) and maintain carefully selected annealing temperatures and times to refine grain size and stabilize microstructural features
generation.structural_mediator: Refined grains and partially recrystallized substructures that promote dislocation interactions
generation.mechanism: The combination of controlled deformation and heat treatment refines and stabilizes the microstructure, which increases dislocation storage capacity for improved strength while preserving ductility through more uniform strain accommodation
generation.predicted_outcome: Both yield strength and elongation will improve relative to the baseline, with strength increasing moderately (e.g., 10–20%) and ductility by a similar margin, though exact values may depend on alloy composition
generation.baseline: Alloy in the as-cast state or subjected only to a single heat treatment, exhibiting coarser grains and lower ductility at a given strength level
generation.boundary: Excessive deformation or annealing temperatures above critical thresholds may lead to abnormal grain growth or embrittlement, limiting the net gain in properties
generation.uncertainty: Long-term thermal stability of the refined microstructure or behavior under complex loading remains insufficiently studied, so the extent of improvement in service conditions is not fully certain

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples, one using the proposed multistep rolling and controlled annealing schedule, and another with a simple single-step heat treatment. Compare tensile strength and ductility at room temperature and elevated temperature.
measurements: Tensile yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation
Fractography analysis to examine microvoid and crack formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples subjected to multistep rolling and controlled annealing do not show any measurable improvement in both yield strength (≥10%) and elongation (≥10%) compared to the single-step treated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] .
